title: Transitional lead-in to enumerated list
description: This latent fires on short introductory phrases (e.g. "Here's why:", "Here's what I think:", "Here are some suggestions:") that immediately precede a numbered or bulleted list, marking the transition from a claim or offer into an enumerated elaboration. It activates most strongly on the canonical, terse "Here's why:" pattern followed directly by "1.", and more weakly on structurally similar lead-ins like "Let's break it down:", "Consider the following:", or "Here are some tips/steps/suggestions:" that also set up a list. It would not activate on the list items themselves, on similar phrases that aren't followed by an enumeration, or on unrelated conversational openers/questions (e.g. "What do you think, OP?", "Don't be silly!") that don't function as a segue into structured content.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (predominantly '2', but also '3', '4', '5', '6') that serve as list-item or step markers, typically followed by a period and often ending a short enumerated line. It activates on the numeric digit itself within enumerated lists, outlines, or step-by-step sequences, largely independent of the surrounding topic content. It would not activate on numbers embedded in prose as quantities, dates, or measurements, nor on ordinal words like 'second' or 'third' written out in full -- the trigger is specifically the bare numeral acting as a list/sequence marker.

title: Interpersonal conflict-advice validation
description: This latent fires on advice-column/relationship-advice style text that validates, reframes, or gently critiques a person's feelings and behavior in an interpersonal conflict (e.g., 'It's reasonable to want...', 'However, that doesn't excuse...', 'Don't let X dictate your decisions'). It activates on sentences that acknowledge someone's perspective or emotions, weigh both sides of a dispute, point out inconsiderate behavior, or offer communication/boundary-setting guidance in the context of relationships, family, or conflict resolution (often in a therapeutic or 'AITA'-style advice register). It does not activate on neutral factual statements, procedural instructions unrelated to interpersonal dynamics (e.g., listing organizations, laundry tips), or narrative descriptions of events that lack this evaluative, advice-giving or validating stance toward someone's feelings/actions.

title: Suggested resource/activity list items
description: This latent fires on bolded or bulleted list items that recommend a specific avenue, resource, platform, or activity as an actionable suggestion, typically in advice-generating text (e.g., 'Join online communities', 'Volunteer', 'Attend school events', 'Use platforms like X'). It activates strongly on the imperative/gerund-headed bullet label plus a colon-elaboration naming concrete options (websites, apps, organizations, event types), reflecting the structural pattern of enumerated recommendation lists rather than any single topic. It does not activate on narrative sentences, explanations of reasoning/motivation, direct dialogue, or advice phrased as full prose sentences without the list-item/label structure, even if they discuss the same topics (e.g., volunteering, socializing, online communities) in a discursive rather than enumerated recommendation format.

title: Empathetic validation in advice-giving
description: This latent fires on short, affect-laden statements typical of advice or support contexts, especially ones that validate, affirm, or morally endorse the reader's feelings or actions ('It's incredibly brave...', 'You took a stand...', 'We can work through this together'). It also picks up related advice-genre fragments like requirement/condition clauses and short directive or rhetorical phrases that appear in the same supportive, second-person coaching register. It is not simply about emotional topics (e.g., grief, abuse, money) but about the stance of a supportive interlocutor reassuring, praising, or guiding someone through a personal situation. Sentences that are purely descriptive, factual, or narrative without this validating/advisory second-person framing would not activate it.

title: Self-care and emotional well-being advice
description: This latent fires on imperative or reminder-style statements urging the reader to prioritize their own emotional well-being, practice self-care, be kind/patient with themselves, or recognize they deserve respect and safety. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic directive phrases (often bolded headers or bullet-point openers like 'Take care of yourself', 'Practice self-care', 'Prioritize your own emotional well-being', 'Be kind to yourself') that appear in advice-giving contexts such as relationship or mental-health guidance. It also activates on isolated fragments and short affirming phrases (e.g. 'Be patient', 'Think', 'Credit') that share the same terse, reassuring, imperative cadence even without full self-care content. It would not activate on descriptive, narrative, or analytical sentences that discuss emotions or relationships without issuing a directive toward self-focused care, nor on advice directed at caring for others rather than oneself.

title: Closing reminder/advice discourse marker
description: This latent fires on the discourse-marking words that open concluding, advice-giving sentences in supportive/therapeutic or self-help style text — especially 'Remember,' 'Remember that,' and 'Ultimately, the decision is yours' as summarizing or reassuring transitions. It activates most strongly on the bare marker itself (just 'Remember,' or 'Ultimately,') before any advice content is even given, and also fires (more weakly) on fuller sentences that use these markers to introduce a piece of reassurance, personal-agency statement, or value reminder (e.g. about relationships, boundaries, well-being). It would not activate on sentences giving similar advice without this specific framing device (e.g. 'It's important to consider...' or 'You should prioritize...') or on factual/narrative sentences lacking a wrap-up/reminder cue word, since the latent tracks the discourse-marker function rather than the advice content itself.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral marking a list item, typically at the start of a bulleted or numbered enumeration (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.'), often followed by bold formatting markup. It activates most strongly on isolated numeral+period tokens that begin sequential list entries, especially in the middle of enumerations (2, 3, 4) rather than the very first item, and co-occurs with contexts like tips, resources, or step-by-step breakdowns. It does not activate on prose sentences that merely mention numbers or quantities in running text, nor on the introductory sentence preceding a list (e.g., 'Here are some tips:'); rather it specifically tracks the structural token that delimits each new list entry.

title: Empathetic advice-column framing
description: This latent fires on the rhetorical scaffolding typical of advice/relationship-forum responses (e.g., Reddit AITA or Dear Abby style replies): framing a personal dilemma as an 'age-old conundrum,' validating the asker's feelings, offering reassurance ('You're NTA', 'Absolutely', 'It's understandable'), or transitioning into advice with phrases like 'Let's break it down' or 'Here are some points in your favor.' It activates most strongly on stock empathetic/validating openers and cliché dilemma-naming phrases ('The age-old debate about...', 'The classic ... scenario!'), and more weakly on other empathetic acknowledgments, judgment verdicts, and conversational connectors within advice-giving text. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, technical instructions, or narrative content that lacks this validating, dilemma-framing advice-column voice, even if the topic is similar (e.g., a plain description of a relationship problem without the empathetic/verdict framing).

title: Interpersonal advice-giving statements
description: This latent fires on sentences that function as advice, validation, or interpretive commentary within a personal-advice or relationship-counseling context—e.g., imperative suggestions ('Ask permission', 'Listen to her', 'Try to pack light'), validating assessments of the reader's or another party's feelings/behavior ('This is understandable', 'You're honoring her wishes'), and bolded advice-column style headers introducing a tip. It activates strongly on second-person or imperative constructions that frame guidance, reassurance, or evaluative judgment about interpersonal situations (family, relationships, work conflicts, etc.), including brief clauses that explain the rationale or expected effect of a suggested action ('This encourages your child to repeat the behavior'). It would not activate on purely factual, narrative, or descriptive sentences lacking an advisory or evaluative stance toward a person's behavior or feelings, such as neutral statements of fact or third-person storytelling without guidance or judgment.

title: Empathetic validation opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic empathy-signaling phrases that an advice-giving assistant uses to open a response—stock expressions like 'I'm so sorry to hear that,' 'I totally understand how you're feeling,' 'I completely get what you mean,' or 'It sounds like you're feeling frustrated.' It activates most strongly on compact, self-contained validation statements that acknowledge the user's emotion or perspective before any substantive advice is given, especially exclamatory or templated forms ('I totally get...!', 'I'm so sorry...'). It activates more weakly but still noticeably on longer sentences embedding similar validating language within a larger clause (e.g., 'It's completely understandable that you're feeling frustrated and anxious about the situation'). It does not activate on purely informational, argumentative, or advice-content sentences that lack this empathetic acknowledgment framing (e.g., factual suggestions, verdicts like 'you're not the asshole,' or neutral questions), even if they occur in the same emotionally supportive conversational context.

title: Empathetic framing exclamations in advice text
description: This latent fires on short, punchy rhetorical phrases that an advice-giving assistant uses to frame or validate a situation before elaborating—either exclamatory labels for a universal dilemma ("The age-old debate!", "The elusive calmness!", "The conundrum!") or brief affirming/validating remarks ("That's commendable.", "You're strong and capable.", "That's frustrating!"). It activates most strongly on these terse, often exclamation-marked, standalone framing sentences that name or normalize the reader's problem/emotion in a relatable, slightly cliché way, and also on nearby reassuring statements of the reader's virtue or capability. It does not activate on longer explanatory or argumentative sentences that provide substantive reasoning, factual content, or multi-clause advice detail, even within the same advice-column context—those carry other latents tied to content/argument structure rather than this stylistic validation/labeling move.

title: List-introduction header
description: This latent fires on the introductory phrase that precedes an enumerated or bulleted list of suggestions, ideas, or steps -- e.g. 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Try:', 'Here's why:', 'Consider:' -- especially when immediately followed by a numbered marker like '1.' or a bolded lead-in. It activates most strongly on these short formulaic lead-in lines themselves rather than on the substantive content of the list items that follow. It also activates more weakly on some individual list-item bullet points (e.g. 'Draw, paint, or create digital art'), likely due to their structural position within a list, but the strongest activation is reserved for the header/preamble sentence that announces the list. It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences giving advice or reflection that are not structured as or introducing an enumerated list, even if they share similar advice-giving content (e.g. 'Practice self-care' as a stand-alone reflective statement rather than a list header).

title: Validating the user's feelings and boundaries in interpersonal advice
description: This latent fires on advice-column style statements that validate the reader's emotions, rights, or boundaries in interpersonal conflicts — e.g., 'You deserve better,' 'It's unfair that...,' 'You're just asking for respect,' or framing another person's behavior as controlling, dismissive, or boundary-violating. It activates on second-person ('you') assertions that legitimize the reader's feelings/actions as reasonable, or that name another party's behavior as disrespectful, manipulative, or unfair, typically in the context of relationship, family, or social-conflict advice. It also fires on rhetorical questions probing motives ('Is she trying to prove something?') and reflective prompts used in this same therapeutic-advice register. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, procedural lists (e.g., business structures, tax rules), or descriptive/narrative content lacking an evaluative stance toward someone's feelings or rights.
